name: Full manscaping routine

lead: A full manscaping routine grooms chest, abdomen, underarms, groin and legs together, from light trimming to full removal, for a tidier, more groomed appearance. The change is visible at once and the practice is widespread. The term dates from about 2003, though male body-hair grooming is much older.

It is discussed in looksmaxxing and style circles as part of overall presentation, often alongside skin care. No clinical trials have tested manscaping as a package; research covers individual hair-removal methods and their side effects.

paras: Hair is shortened with trimmers or clippers, cut at the surface with razors or chemical depilatories, or removed from the root by waxing or sugaring, with laser or electrolysis for longer-lasting reduction. The method chosen determines how long results last.

Reported problems of hair removal in general include skin inflammation, minor burns, ingrown hairs, bumps, folliculitis and scarring. Waxing can cause skin lifting in people using certain medications or topical retinoids. A 2021 Cochrane review found razors probably raise surgical-site infection risk compared with clippers or cream when used before surgery.

chain: Trim or remove body hair by region
angle.text: A full manscaping routine trims or removes hair across the chest, abdomen, underarms, groin and legs for a neat, consistent, groomed look. The result is visible at once, and risks depend on the removal method used.

lead: Manscaping is a portmanteau of 'man' and 'landscaping' that refers to trimming, shaping or removing male body hair. The earliest known use of the term is dated to 2003.[1] A 'full manscaping routine' is an informal label for grooming several body regions in one regimen, typically chest, abdomen, underarms, groin and legs, sometimes alongside skin care.

Grooming body hair has a long history: ancient Egyptian and Greek athletes are described as trimming or removing it, possibly for competitive reasons in sports such as wrestling and swimming, and the practice has revived in recent decades for aesthetic and sexual reasons.[1] Hair removal in general is a broad field spanning shaving, depilatory creams, waxing, sugaring, laser and electrolysis.[2]
No trials have tested a full manscaping routine as an intervention. Published research addresses individual methods and their complications, summarised below.
infobox: Trimming, shaving, depilatory cream, waxing, sugaring, laser

paras: Male grooming as a whole covers hair, beard, skin and body care. Within it, body-hair work is one strand alongside products such as lotions, fragrances and sunscreen, and procedures such as laser hair removal.[1]

Methods differ in how long results last. Waxing and sugaring remove hair from the root, with results lasting from several days to several weeks, while depilatory creams dissolve hair at the surface and their effect lasts hours to days.[2] Trimming simply shortens hair.

Wikipedia notes that male removal of body hair has grown in popularity in some Western subcultures, and that shaving the pubic area is common among men for aesthetic reasons, though the article supplies no statistics.[2] Market estimates put the global male grooming industry at about US$81.2 billion by 2024.[1]
Male body-hair removal is also discussed in terms of sport, with athletes in some disciplines shaving for perceived performance or presentation reasons.[1]

Documented problems of hair removal include skin inflammation, minor burns, lesions, scarring, ingrown hairs, bumps and folliculitis.[2] Ingrown hairs are most common in people with coarse or curly hair and in areas that are shaved or waxed, including the beard, legs and pubic region.[3]

Waxing can cause pain, redness, minor bleeding and skin lifting. Factors listed as raising the chance of skin lifting include blood thinners, steroids, topical retinoids, recent sunburn or laser treatment, and skin conditions such as eczema or psoriasis.[4]
A 2021 Cochrane review of 25 studies with 8,919 participants found that razors probably increase surgical-site infection risk compared with clippers, hair-removal cream or no removal.[2]

No studies found. Research exists on individual hair-removal methods; for example, a 2006 review of laser and light treatments reported temporary side effects in 9.5% (alexandrite), 28.9% (diode) and 15.3% (intense pulsed light) of patients.[2]

timeline.event: Earliest known use of the term 'manscaping'.[1]
A Lancet report links pre-surgical shaving to higher infection risk, after which clippers become the recommended method.[2]
Cochrane review of 25 studies finds razors probably raise surgical-site infection risk compared with clippers or cream.[2]
